ready1_open_rewrite.rewritten_question_text: Three-digit powers of 2 and 5 are used in this cross-number puzzle. What is the only possible digit for the outlined square? \begin{tabular}{lcl} \textbf{ACROSS} & & \textbf{DOWN} \\ \textbf{2}. $2^m$ & & \textbf{1}. $5^n$ \end{tabular}

ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_question_text: Three-digit powers of 2 and 5 are used in this cross-number puzzle. What is the only possible digit for the outlined square? \begin{tabular}{lcl} \textbf{ACROSS} & & \textbf{DOWN} \\ \textbf{2}. $2^m$ & & \textbf{1}. $5^n$ \end{tabular}
ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The attached figure shows a cross-number grid. On the left side there are three vertically consecutive squares, and the topmost square is labeled 1; the middle-left square is labeled 2. The square labeled 2 extends to the right to form a three-square horizontal entry, and the rightmost square is highlighted with a thicker border. Therefore, Down 1 occupies three squares downward from the upper-left square; Across 2 occupies three squares to the right from the middle-left square; the middle-left square is simultaneously the 2nd position of Down 1 and the 1st position of Across 2, and the highlighted square is the 3rd position of Across 2. Reasoning: Down 1 is a three-digit power of 5. The only three-digit powers of 5 are 125 and 625, and their second digit is both 2. So the middle-left square must be the digit 2, that is, the first digit of Across 2 is 2. Across 2 is a three-digit power of 2. The three-digit powers of 2 are 128, 256, 512; among them only 256 starts with 2. Therefore Across 2 must be 256, and the highlighted third digit is 6.

method.method_draft: Use direct candidate enumeration and intersection matching. First read the image: the clue numbered 1 starts at the top-left square and goes downward for three squares; the clue numbered 2 starts at the middle-left square and goes across for three squares; the outlined square is the rightmost square of the across entry. Therefore the middle-left square is both the 2nd digit of Down 1 and the 1st digit of Across 2, while the outlined square is the 3rd digit of Across 2. From the text, Down 1 is a three-digit power of 5 and Across 2 is a three-digit power of 2. List the three-digit powers of 5: 125 and 625, whose second digit is always 2. Hence Across 2 must begin with digit 2. List the three-digit powers of 2: 128, 256, 512; only 256 begins with 2. The outlined square is the last digit of 256, so it is 6.

method.method_draft: Use exponent bounds and digit-position constraints rather than a full cross table. First read the image: the vertical entry numbered 1 has three cells, and its middle cell is also the first cell of the horizontal entry numbered 2; the outlined square is the third cell of the horizontal entry. From the text, the vertical entry is 5^n and the horizontal entry is 2^m, both three-digit. Since 5^2=25, 5^3=125, 5^4=625, and 5^5=3125, the only possible three-digit powers of 5 have tens digit 2. Thus the first digit of the horizontal power of 2 must be 2. Now bound the three-digit powers of 2: 2^7=128, 2^8=256, 2^9=512, and 2^10=1024, so the only three-digit power of 2 lying between 200 and 299 is 2^8=256. Therefore the outlined third digit is 6.
